draftPackage.centralQuestion: How did one injured engineer survive both1945 atomic bombings, and what does official double recognition mean?
draftPackage.thesis: One injured shipbuilding engineer returned from Hiroshima to his home city, Nagasaki, before the second bombing. His official double-exposure recognition does not make him the only double survivor. His later witness serves remembrance and nuclear abolition.
draftPackage.viewerPayoff: One injured shipbuilding engineer returned from Hiroshima to his home city, Nagasaki, before the second bombing. His official double-exposure recognition does not make him the only double survivor. His later witness serves remembrance and nuclear abolition.

segments.text: He survived an atomic bomb. Three days later, he survived another.
This is Tsutomu Yamaguchi, a Mitsubishi shipbuilding engineer.
August sixth, nineteen forty-five. He was in Hiroshima on business when the United States dropped an atomic bomb.
The next day, he boarded a train. It carried him home to Nagasaki.
On August ninth, he was back at work. He recalled describing Hiroshima to his manager.
Then came another flash. The second atomic bomb had struck.
He survived again. His wife and infant son survived too.
The bombings killed tens of thousands and left lasting suffering.
In two thousand nine, Japan officially recognized his exposure in both cities.
He was not the only double survivor.
He lived until twenty ten, aged ninety-three.
In later years, he urged the world to abolish nuclear weapons.
